newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Albright, Primakov duel over Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Albright, Primakov duel over Bosnia.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, touring Eastern Europe to explain NATO's expansion policy, crossed swords over Bosnia with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Saturday.

During a 19-hour visit by Albright to Russia's former tsarist capital, she and Primakov also discussed the possibility of extending Vienna talks on an updated European conventional arms treaty in a bid to reach a framework accord.

Albright flew to St Petersburg from Slovenia, where she told leaders there was "no stronger candidate" than the small Alpine state for NATO's next round of enlargement even though it was left out in the first round announced this week.

U.S. officials said that during a dinner meeting at a posh St Petersburg restaurant Primakov detailed Russia's objections to NATO's swoop on Thursday on suspected war criminals in Bosnia, denounced by Moscow on Friday as a "cowboy raid".

In the operation by British special forces, a hospital director in the town of Prijedor was arrested and a former police chief was shot dead resisting arrest. Both had been the subject of sealed war crimes indictments by a U.N. tribunal.

Primakov said Russia was worried the action could undermine Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic, whom the West is supporting in a power struggle with former Serb leader Radovan Karadzic, himself indicted for war crimes.

"The secretary's response was essentially that we can't get (the Bosnian Serbs) to turn over war criminals, this is a way to do it, what's your suggestion? He didn't really have an answer," said a U.S. official, speaking anonymously.

The official said the two ministers discussed whether to seek to extend to the end of July Vienna talks on an amended Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty that would take into account changes in Europe since the pact was signed in 1990.
The current round of the 30-nation talks is due to end in mid-month.

Russia is trying to head off what it sees as threats to security from the eastward expansion of NATO, but the West is seeking to stop Russia vetoing the arms holdings of new NATO members through a new CFE treaty.
U.S. officials said Albright and Primakov made little progress, but experts were pursuing discussions into the night before the two ministers meet again on Sunday morning.

A NATO summit in Madrid earlier this week invited Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to apply to join -- a move Primakov on Tuesday called "the biggest mistake in Europe since the end of World War Two".
Officials said he and Albright re-stated their positions on Saturday "and neither of them surprised each other".

In a diplomatic offensive to explain the NATO decision, U.S. President Bill Clinton this week visited Poland and Romania, Defence Secretary William Cohen has been to Hungary, Bulgaria and Ukraine and Albright is touring Slovenia, Russia, Lithuania and the Czech Republic.
Other subjects covered by Albright and Primakov included ways of preventing new Russian arms sales to Iran and ways of re-starting the stalled Middle East peace process, officials said.
The two ministers have developed a considerable personal rapport despite their months of sometimes outspoken duelling over NATO expansion and other issues.

Albright's visit opens a round of diplomatic house calls on Russia by Western foreign ministers. British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook will be in Moscow on Monday and Tuesday. Germany's Klaus Kinkel will discuss NATO with Primakov on Tuesday in the capital.

All are expected to stress a willingness to develop Moscow's cooperation with NATO under a recent charter which seeks to allay Russia's fears over NATO expansion by giving it a say in alliance affairs.
